rationale: A wins because it treats the missing facts as the story instead of wallpapering over them. Its best line, "REI won't say how big its resale business actually is, even as it leans on it for sustainability credit," turns the supplied disclosure gap into a clean accountability angle. B has sharper-sounding business drama, but "public retailers can't easily replicate" and "As outdoor gear floods secondhand apps" are unsupported scaffolding, and unsupported scaffolding is where pitches go to die.
gaps_in_A: "the dividend flows to paying customer-members, not to the employees organizing" is a useful tension, but it needs to stay framed as a question until dividend eligibility and employee/member overlap are confirmed.

"REI's bet: gear resale and repair aren't a sustainability side project, they're core retail infrastructure" overstates REI's intent; the update proves nationwide expansion, not REI's internal strategic framing.
"None of these are pitch-ready yet" is too absolute; the all-store rollout angle could be pitched to trade press with a rollout timeline and a real store/member anecdote.
gaps_in_B: "public retailers can't easily replicate" is an invented competitive claim; the update gives no public-retailer comparison or evidence that ownership structure creates a moat.
"because there are no external shareholders demanding margin protection" smuggles in a finance argument the facts do not support.
"As outdoor gear floods secondhand apps" invents the market condition that makes the counterposition angle work.
"requires trained repair technicians — a skilled, non-automatable role" may be true in the real world, but it is not in the supplied update, and the labor angle leans on it too hard.
